questions.title: How does substantial-evidence review work when the BIA issues a brief, single-member decision?
questions.question_body: The panel says it reviews the BIA’s decision but can consult the IJ’s "more complete explanation" (citing Uanreroro). I’m confused about what that actually means in practice. Does the court treat the IJ’s reasoning as part of the BIA’s rationale, or only as background? When is remand required because the BIA’s decision is too cursory to permit meaningful review, versus when can the court lean on the IJ’s findings to uphold the BIA?

questions.title: Why didn’t the armed threats and the incident with the child count as past persecution?
questions.question_body: The court repeats that "threats alone" are insufficient, but here there were two armed confrontations (guns brandished, orders to leave, death threats), an assault on a factory employee while searching for petitioners, and a man physically grabbing the son with a hand over his mouth before the child ran away. The IJ found petitioners credible. How does the Tenth Circuit distinguish these facts from cases where cumulative threats and intimidation cross the line into persecution, especially where there is some physical contact (even if brief) and weapons involved? Also, does harm to a third party (the assaulted employee) ever count toward the ‘cumulative’ persecution analysis?

questions.title: In a mixed-motive case, how did the court conclude politics was only ‘tangential’ given the explicit references to the Liberal Party?
questions.question_body: The opinion acknowledges a brochure saying "death to snitches from Liberal Party" and that the men called petitioners "snitches" who were "in politics." Yet the court treated the campaign-related threats as not tied to Don Rafa and emphasized the later property-dispute motive as predominant. What evidentiary showing is needed to establish that political opinion was at least one central reason when some threats are political in content but the persecutor may also be retaliating for anti-crime or personal-conflict reasons? Do applicants have to identify the same persecutor behind all incidents to link earlier political threats into the nexus analysis?

questions.title: What counts as adequate ‘reporting’ to prove the government is unable or unwilling to protect?
questions.question_body: Petitioners told at least one patrol officer, who allegedly said officers were part of the problem and told them to leave, but they didn’t file formal complaints or escalate beyond the neighborhood. The panel says that’s insufficient and points to prior police search attempts at the property as evidence of state willingness. Practically, what steps satisfy the notice-and-opportunity requirement in the Tenth Circuit—does verbally informing a patrol officer count? When is failure to report excused as dangerous or futile, and what kind of record evidence (e.g., country reports, prior retaliation against complainants) is needed to meet that exception?

questions.title: Who bears the burden on internal relocation absent past persecution, and did the panel apply the right factors?
questions.question_body: My understanding is that without a past-persecution finding, the applicant bears the burden to show relocation would be unreasonable under 8 C.F.R. § 1208.13(b)(3). Here, the court relied on facts like family remaining unharmed in Colombia, three weeks safely spent in the countryside, and threats that said to leave the neighborhood (not the country). Are those facts alone typically sufficient to find relocation reasonable? How should factors like the applicants’ children, economic disruption, and alleged nationwide reach of the persecutors be weighed, and did the court treat any of those as forfeited due to inadequate briefing?

questions.title: How does alleged ‘alignment’ between private persecutors and the ruling party factor into nexus and the state-action analysis?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes allegations that Don Rafa is a narco-guerrilla leader "politically aligned" with President Petro, but concludes the record doesn’t show persecutors were closely associated with the government, pointing to prior law-enforcement searches of the property. What kind of proof would establish a sufficient connection—ideological sympathy, selective non-enforcement, bribery, documented collusion, or something else—to (a) help satisfy nexus to political opinion, and/or (b) show the government is unwilling or unable to control private actors?

questions.title: Does the difference in nexus standards between asylum and withholding matter here?
questions.question_body: The panel says petitioners necessarily fail withholding because they failed to establish asylum eligibility. I know asylum requires a ‘well-founded fear’ and ‘one central reason’ for nexus, while some circuits apply an ‘a reason’ nexus standard for withholding. What is the Tenth Circuit’s current rule on withholding nexus? Did the panel’s conclusion rest on the lack of a well-founded fear (which would automatically defeat the higher ‘more likely than not’ standard for withholding), or did its nexus holding for asylum also control the withholding analysis?
